messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Arjun Patel had worked for an international aid organization in his early thirties, sent into a war zone to help with relief coordination after bombardments had torn apart a neighborhood of apartments, a clinic, and the small cemetery behind the mosque. One afternoon, while he was moving between damaged buildings with local staff, a shelling strike ignited fuel and debris nearby. The smoke came fast and thick, carrying the sharp, acrid smell of fire that seemed to cling to his clothes and hair. In the chaos, people were shouting, some with anger and some with grief, and Arjun found himself trying to shepherd frightened families toward cover while also hearing the cries from the cemetery side where several graves had been disturbed. He remembers pieces of that day in fragments: the blast, the smell, a body on the ground, someone yelling at him, his own hands shaking in front of his face. Even now, when he tries to tell the story, the sequence slips apart; he cannot put the memories in the right order, and that confusion only deepens his sense that something unforgivable happened while he stood there.

Since returning home, Arjun has found that the smell of smoke or fire can pull him back in an instant. A passing car with a burnt engine, food left too long on the stove, even incense near a temple during a family visit can make his chest tighten and his mind go blank with the feeling that he is back in that ruined street. When that happens he covers his face with his hands without thinking, as if hiding from what he has remembered, and he gets away from the source of the smell as quickly as possible. The cues do more than startle him; they set off a surge of danger that feels immediate and real, and at the same time the smell or sight opens the memory of that afternoon before he can steady himself. In those moments he is flooded with the thought that if smoke can still find him anywhere, then he is never really out of reach of what happened. He avoids the site of the event whenever work or travel might bring him near that district, and he steers clear of funerals, cemeteries, or any grief-related gathering because the sight of mourning families and disturbed earth brings the day rushing back. He has also begun avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful, turning down invitations and keeping celebrations at arm’s length, as though allowing himself any relief would be reckless. At home in his role as a tax consultant, he has become more withdrawn in the office, declining lunch outings and leaving earlier so he does not have to linger in situations that feel emotionally exposed. Staying away feels like the only sensible response to him, because once the trigger has landed he experiences the world as dangerous all over again. In that state even ordinary days at the office feel like a place where something could go wrong, so he keeps himself small and moves quickly through the workday.

Arjun had come to believe that the world no longer worked according to any rules he could trust. What frightened him most was not only what happened there, but what it seemed to mean about him: he should have protected others and failed. That belief rose up whenever he remembered the people he could not save, and the shame felt physical, as if his body returned to the same crouched position it had taken behind a wall while the shelling continued. The more he recalls that day, the more certain he becomes that he is set apart from other people, carrying something damaged and dishonorable that they would not understand. Those thoughts do not stay abstract; they shape where he goes and what he allows himself to feel. If he notices smoke, hears about a funeral, or senses anger in another person’s voice—even when it is calm—he pulls back, covers his face, and keeps away, as if distance can keep him from being overwhelmed again. Once he had decided that he was unsafe to himself and inadequate to others, almost any reminder could confirm it — a whiff of smoke, a raised voice, a mention of the dead. The more certain he became that he had failed and could not trust his own judgement, the more every cue seemed to carry a warning that something terrible was about to happen.

Yet the distance has not brought relief. By avoiding the event site and anything that resembles the loss, Arjun has found himself thinking about it more, not less; the memories arrive with less warning, and when they do, the shame lands harder. He notices his body tensing in the middle of ordinary tasks, and the same sense of helplessness returns with it. The more he hides and retreats, the more isolated and set apart he feels, which only confirms his belief that something about him has been permanently altered. At night this is worst: the house feels less safe than in daylight, and ordinary sounds—a door closing, a bicycle bell outside, his wife moving in the kitchen—make him jump. He lies awake scanning for danger, his attention broken and scattered, and the fatigue bleeds into his work, where concentration has become difficult enough that he rereads the same figures over and over. Not speaking about it and not going back there has left the memory undisturbed, so it comes back vivid and intact, often at the very moments he is trying hardest not to think about it. Each return of the image seems to prove his worst fear about himself, that there is something permanently damaged in him, and that proof keeps his mind fixed on danger long after the original event.

His wife has tried to pull him into family dinners and weekend plans, but he often refuses, especially if they are meant to be cheerful. He is afraid that if he lets himself feel hopeful, it will only make the fall worse. The avoidance has narrowed his life, and with each retreat his belief that he failed to protect others and cannot trust the world becomes more solid. He finally sought help after a night when the smell of smoke from a neighbor’s cooking fire sent him into a panic, he spent hours awake listening for sounds outside, and the next morning he made an error at work because he could not concentrate. Arjun came in hoping to stop feeling hunted by reminders, and fearing that if nothing changes he will remain trapped in the shame of that day, unable to be present with his wife, his work, or any future that might still be possible. The more he pulled away from dinners, celebrations, and ordinary closeness, the more his life became a map of places and situations he could no longer tolerate. Having never stayed long enough to discover that those moments were safe, he experienced the danger as ongoing, and that made even a normal evening at home feel like a test he might fail.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows negative beliefs about himself, but no paragraph clearly states that these appraisals cause or intensify the triggers/reminders themselves.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette links triggers to memory and threat, but it does not clearly state that feeling threatened drives the traumatic memory to return.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette describes avoidance and withdrawal, but no paragraph clearly says these maladaptive strategies cause the memory to become more active or intrusive.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more he recalls that day, the more certain he becomes that he is set apart from other people, carrying something damaged and dishonorable that they would not understand.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That conviction made the smallest cues feel loaded for him: a thin ribbon of smoke from a kitchen vent, a funeral notice, even an angry tone across a room could snag his attention and seem to announce danger before anyone else in the room had noticed anything at all. Because he already believed the world had gone wrong and that his own judgement could not be trusted, ordinary reminders did not stay ordinary for long; they became proof that the threat was still near.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more he hides and retreats, the more isolated and set apart he feels, which only confirms his belief that something about him has been permanently altered.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That persistent sense of danger kept pulling the day back toward him at night, as if his mind could not afford to let the memory sit untouched while he stayed on alert. On the evenings when the house felt least safe, the scene returned most vividly, not because he chose it, but because the threat still felt unfinished.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more he pulled away from dinners, celebrations, and ordinary closeness, the more his life became a map of places and situations he could no longer tolerate.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
By refusing to talk about it and by keeping anything that might remind him at a distance, he had never really put the memory anywhere; it stayed in him, undisturbed and intact, and when it surfaced it came back with the same force it had carried in the first place. The effort of holding it away seemed to have kept it close.
<<<END>>>
